text:
We question again the negative attitude toward ORV use displayed in the writing of this environmental statement. The fact is that "no area of public lands is free from potential damage by . . ." almost any use. To suggest that all sand dune areas and all snow fields are "fragile and susceptible land forms" is to not understand that the next breeze or the next snowfall can completely mitigate the environmental impact of ORV tracks on sand or snow.
We agree with the use of soil erodibility appraisals in helping to identify areas for appropriate ORV use; but suggest that they are needed also in defining areas for many other traditional uses such as grazing, mining and timber. Again, the answer is not so much "open" or "close," but "manage."
Pages 15 and 16: The discussion of biological impacts sounds like all populations and species of wildlife have had a run-in with ORV's. We suspect that the discussion applies more realistically to isolated instances, as with other uses of the public lands. The writers and readers of such impact statements need to be reminded that even the revered backpackers can "disturb" wildlife.
Page 17: We see no reason to assume that properly managed use of ORV's would have a "minor adverse impact on the economic effects of outdoor recreation." To the contrary, safe and sane provision of ORV opportunities could increase the positive economic effect because of the increased interest and use which would be attracted by well-managed areas. As the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation should know, most ORV users are responsible individuals looking for protection of their "investment" as well.
Page 18: We question the use of the phrase "often at high speeds" when referring to exploring of areas. Anyone familiar with most ORV use would know that most exploring is at a leisurely pace and that the racing event, which is usually held at an appropriate site and under appropriate regulations, is at high speed; but is far from "exploring," and is not the kind of activity pursued by the average ORV user.
Page 19: We agree that the time when any user can use the public lands whenever and wherever he wishes is long gone. All must accept the idea that their use of public lands will of necessity be managed.
We wonder why trails, parking areas, rest stops and other developments are "unsightly" when associated with ORV use, but not an unmanageable problem when associated with camping, picnicking or backpacking use.
Page 20: We question the idea that concentrating vehicles and people in designated areas will help the situation. It could cause more environmental damage unless there are enough such areas, and they are large enough in terms of their capacity.
We think that ORV designated areas should be rated similar to ski runs: (1) beginning, (2) intermediate, (3) advanced, etc, so users can match their degree of skill with the terrain.
